Zirconia is consumed by carbon through the well-characterized carbothermal reduction reaction: 3C(s) + ZrO₂(s) = ZrC(s) + 2CO(g) (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 2-3). The crystallite growth follows a "contracting volume" model where the ZrC shell grows inward from the surface of ZrO₂ particles (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 5-7). These findings demonstrate that zirconia crucibles or insulation in direct contact with graphite or carbon-rich environments at temperatures above ~1200 °C will be progressively consumed, making ZrO₂ a poor choice for long-duration containment against carbon at the temperatures of interest.

## 5. Tantalum–Boron Nitride Interface Degradation

Boron nitride is commonly employed in high-temperature furnace assemblies as a separator, insulator, or structural element alongside tantalum crucibles. While BN possesses excellent thermal shock resistance and chemical inertness in many environments, direct prolonged contact between Ta and BN at temperatures above ~1700 °C can lead to interfacial reaction. The strong oxygen affinity of tantalum, with a binding energy of Q_O = 166–179 kcal/g-atom (glebovsky2015physicalandtechnological pages 10-13), means that tantalum in contact with oxide ceramics such as MgO can abstract oxygen from the ceramic at high temperatures. At temperatures from approximately 1200 °C upward in vacuum environments, tantalum reacts with residual oxygen to form volatile oxide species, principally TaO(g) and TaO₂(g) (inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 30-35). Tantalum is one of the strongest oxygen getters among the refractory metals. # Summary

This excerpt discusses hetero-epitaxial growth of AlN crystals on SiC substrates at high temperatures (~1900°C) using the PVT technique. Key findings include:

**Hole Defect Formation**: Micro-pipes in SiC substrates propagate into growing AlN, causing holes up to ~100 µm in thin crystals and macro-holes of 200 µm. Decomposition of SiC occurs simultaneously with AlN growth; holes deeper than 600 µm originate from the SiC substrate itself.

**Crucible Materials**: TaC crucibles are preferred over tungsten (which forms "low-temperature eutectics such as tungsten silicides") because they prevent Si-W reactions. However, **TaC crucibles in graphite heater environments naturally accompany diffusion of Si and C into growing AlN crystals**, introducing impurities.

**Crystal Coloration**: Oxygen contamination causes yellow coloration and oxynitride formation, decreasing thermal conductivity. The excerpt notes that even modest impurity concentrations affect crystal quality and optical properties.

The document does not directly address the comprehensive chemical compatibility review requested.

# Summary

This ORNL report from 1968 by H. Inouye reviews interactions of refractory metals with active gases at temperatures from 600-2000°C and pressures from 10^-5 to 10^-7 torr. The document establishes that "contamination, degassing, decarburization, and sublimation reactions occur between the refractory metals and absorbed gases." 

Key findings include that reaction rates are governed by "the deviation of the interstitial concentration of the refractory alloy from the equilibrium concentration dictated by the temperature and pressure of the active gas." The report systematically addresses gas-metal equilibria, reaction kinetics, decarburization, sublimation, and control methods. Major impurities in inert gases and vacuum systems include "H₂O, O₂, N₂, CO, CO₂, H₂, and CH₄." The extent of interstitial instability can be determined from "the pressure-temperature-composition relationship" when gas pressure is known at specific temperatures.

# Summary

This excerpt discusses theoretical and experimental aspects of removing interstitial impurities (carbon and oxygen) from high-purity refractory metals through vacuum processing. The author describes a complex heterogeneous removal process consisting of four elementary steps: "diffusion transition of impurities from the volume of metal to the surface layer," transition across the metal surface interface, recombination of adsorbed atoms, and desorption into gas phase or vacuum. The text presents a kinetic analysis using a system of conservation equations (equations 1-4) involving bulk impurity content (N), surface layer content, and flux densities. A "quasi-stationary approximation" simplifies the complex system by assuming impurity flows quickly adapt. However, the excerpt focuses on molybdenum, tungsten, and niobium purification rather than the specific refractory materials (tantalum, graphite, boron nitride, magnesia, alumina, zirconia) and high-temperature compatibility issues requested in the question.

The excerpt discusses reaction kinetics governing gas-metal contamination at high temperatures. contexts.context: This excerpt presents a PhD dissertation studying high-temperature oxidation of tantalum carbide-hafnium carbide solid solutions synthesized via spark plasma sintering. The work synthesizes five TaC-HfC compositions (pure HfC, T20H80, T50H50, T80H20, and pure TaC), achieving near-full density without sintering aids. X-ray diffraction confirmed solid solution formation. Samples were tested under oxygen-rich plasma flow at approximately 2800°C with gas velocities exceeding 300 m/s. Results show T50H50 exhibited superior oxidation resistance, reducing oxide scale thickness by >90% compared to pure TaC and >85% compared to pure HfC after 5-minute tests. A novel Ta₂Hf₆O₁₇ phase and HfO₂ scaffold structures filled with molten Ta₂O₅ contributed to improved oxidation performance.

# Summary

This excerpt describes synthesis methods for zirconium carbide (ZrC) and hafnium carbide (HfC) through solution-based precursors and carbothermal reduction, but does not address the high-temperature chemical compatibility review requested.

The text details: zirconium n-propoxide mixed with acetylacetone at molar ratios of 0.25–0.33, refluxed at 130–195°C, then partially hydrolyzed with HNO₃/Zr ratios of 0.04–0.27 and H₂O/Zr ratio of 24. Glycerol or phenolic resin were added to control C/Zr ratios. Pyrolysis occurred at 800–1100°C in argon, followed by heat treatment at 1200–1800°C. The idealized carbothermal reduction reaction is: "3C(s) + ZrO₂(s) = ZrC(s) + 2CO(g)". C/Zr molar ratios in pyrolyzed samples ranged from ~1.6 to ~2.4 by varying HNO₃/Zr molar ratios (0.42 to 0.12).

The excerpt focuses on synthesis methodology rather than chemical compatibility among refractory crucible/susceptor materials.

# Summary

This excerpt from Baud et al. (2003) presents thermodynamic calculations of vaporization behavior for aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) and yttrium oxide (Y₂O₃) at high temperatures (1200-2300 K). 

For Al₂O₃, the study confirms congruent evaporation with the predominant reaction: "Al₂O₃(s) → 2Al(g) + 3O(g)" where Al(g) and O(g) are the main gas species. The calculations use Gibbs energy data from the SGTE database and match experimental measurements from Drowart, Burns, and Farber.

For Y₂O₃, congruent vaporization occurs with YO(g), YO₂(g), and O(g) as major species, though experimental literature indicates YO(g) dominates. The excerpt notes discrepancies: measured data shows no detected YO₂(g), contradicting calculated partial pressures that predict this species at levels above 10⁻⁶.

# Summary

The excerpt discusses decarburization and sublimation mechanisms in refractory metals at high temperatures. Decarburization of niobium-zirconium alloys becomes significant above 1200°C through carbon-oxygen interactions forming carbon monoxide removed by vacuum pumps. The decarburization rate is "governed by the diffusion rate of carbon in the alloy," with CO generation increasing with temperature as carbon diffusivity increases. 

For sublimation, Figures 18-20 show volatile oxide formation from oxygen reactions with tungsten, molybdenum, and tantalum across wide temperature ranges. Generation rates are "temperature dependent" and characteristically pass through maxima. Tungsten and molybdenum show constant sublimation rates at given temperature-pressure conditions with linear extent increase over time, while "the sublimation rate of tantalum varies markedly with time." The excerpt focuses on tungsten, molybdenum, and niobium-zirconium systems rather than the specific materials (tantalum, graphite, boron nitride, magnesia, alumina, zirconia) requested in the question.

# Summary

This excerpt examines thermodynamic vaporization behavior of SiC-Al₂O₃ and SiC-Al₂O₃/Y₂O₃ mixtures in open systems at high temperatures (1200-2300 K). Key findings include: pure Al₂O₃ and Y₂O₃ evaporate congruently, while pure SiC vaporizes non-congruently producing graphite. The SiC-Al₂O₃ mixture evaporates congruently via: "2 SiC(s) + Al₂O₃(s) + Al₂O(g) → 2 SiO(g) + 2 CO(g) + 4 Al(g)," with composition shifting toward pure SiC in SiC-rich samples and pure Al₂O₃ in Al₂O₃-rich samples. The paper notes prior studies identified major gas species including SiO(g), CO(g), Al₂O(g), and Al(g), and discusses liquid phase formation from Al₂O₃-Al₄C₃ and SiC-Al₄C₃ eutectics between 2220-2273 K with excess carbon present.

# Summary

This excerpt discusses thermodynamic analysis of vaporization and mass transport in ceramic systems at high temperatures. The key framework involves calculating atomic fluxes of elements escaping a system using the Hertz-Knudsen relation for effusion (Equation 2): dNi/dt = √(2πisCRMiT) = F(i). For compounds with congruent vaporization, atomic flux ratios are linked to mole fractions in the condensed phase (Equation 1). contexts.context: Tantalum, as a Group 5 refractory metal, exhibits significant oxygen removal capability at high temperatures. In solid state, tantalum desorbs oxygen primarily as monoxides and suboxides with an evaporation ratio of 28-42, making purification from oxygen possible through high-temperature vacuum annealing. At temperatures above its melting point (T > Tm), tantalum demonstrates exceptional deoxidation potential with an evaporation ratio reaching 2,000-3,000, indicating intensive oxygen removal from the molten state in vacuum. Tantalum's reaction with chemisorbed oxygen occurs through the formation and desorption of metal oxides (TaO and TaO2), with the desorption of monoxide (TaO) being the primary mechanism at low surface coverage. The binding energy of oxygen on tantalum is relatively high (QO = 166-179 kcal/g-atom), reflecting strong oxygen affinity characteristic of Group 5 metals.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses tantalum's reaction with oxygen at high temperatures. Unlike tungsten and molybdenum, tantalum's sublimation rate varies significantly with time rather than remaining constant. The formation of volatile TaO(g) oxide increases continuously until reaching saturation. This behavior results from competition between oxygen dissolving into the tantalum metal and formation of volatile tantalum oxide. As oxygen pressure increases, more oxygen dissolves into the metal until saturation is reached, after which the sublimation rate becomes constant. At very high temperatures, particularly when tantalum is exposed to oxygen sources such as oxides or ceramic materials, both the oxygen saturation and sublimation processes can become serious problems causing material losses over extended reaction times. The excerpt indicates this is particularly concerning in practical applications involving high temperatures.

This two-stage crucible approach avoids direct interactions between tungsten or tantalum metals with silicon and carbon, which would otherwise form low-melting eutectics that could compromise crystal quality.

contexts.context: The document describes SiC-Al2O3 vaporization behavior through thermodynamic analysis. The main vaporization reaction for SiC-Al2O3 mixtures is: 2 SiC(s) + Al2O3(s) + Al2O(g) → 2 SiO(g) + 2 CO(g) + 4 Al(g), which occurs congruently overall though the mixture composition changes over time. A simpler reaction also occurs: SiC(s) + Al2O3(s) ↔ Al2O(g) + SiO(g) + CO(g). During high-temperature sintering, two scenarios exist: (1) Without excess carbon, a liquid Al or Si phase forms between 2373-2423 K, with liquid potentially produced from Mullite Al6Si2O13 decomposition above 2140 K. (2) With excess carbon present, liquid phases form due to Al2O3-Al4C3 or SiC-Al4C3 eutectics between 2220-2273 K, and an Al2O3-Al4C3-SiC liquid phase is also possible. These liquid phases support the sintering process.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Review high-temperature (1700-2500 C) chemical compatibility among refractory materials used as crucibles and susceptors: tantalum, graphite/carbon, boron nitride, magnesia (MgO), alumina, and zirconia. Include carburization of tantalum (TaC formation), alumina-carbon reactions and eutectics near 1800 C, carbothermal reduction/consumption of zirconia by carbon, Ta-BN and Ta-MgO interface degradation, interdiffusion and vapor transport (Ta deposition on ceramic specimens), and oxygen gettering by tantalum. Cite high-quality sources with bibtex.

# High-Temperature Chemical Compatibility Among Refractory Crucible and Susceptor Materials (1700–2500 °C)

## 1. Introduction

High-temperature processing of advanced materials — including sublimation growth of AlN and SiC single crystals, sintering of ultra-high-temperature ceramics, and zone refining of refractory metals — routinely employs crucibles, susceptors, and containment made from tantalum, graphite/carbon, boron nitride (BN), magnesia (MgO), alumina (Al₂O₃), and zirconia (ZrO₂). At temperatures of 1700–2500 °C, none of these materials can be regarded as universally inert; pairwise chemical reactions including carburization, carbothermal reduction, eutectic liquid formation, oxygen gettering, and vapor-phase transport can compromise crucible integrity, contaminate growing crystals, and alter the local thermochemical environment. The following sections review the most important compatibility issues.

The summary of all material pair interactions is presented in the table below.

| Material Pair | Temperature Range (°C) | Reaction/Interaction | Key Products | Practical Implications |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Tantalum + Graphite/Carbon | ~1700–2500 | Reactive diffusion/carburization of Ta in C-rich environments; pre-carbonization intentionally forms protective carbide layers on Ta crucibles, typically TaC/Ta2C, and suppresses direct Ta–Si and Ta–Al eutectic attack | TaC, Ta2C, sometimes TaCN during nitride growth service | Bare Ta is not compatible with graphite at these temperatures for long exposure; carburized/TaC-coated Ta is much more stable and is therefore used as crucible or liner material in high-T nitride crystal growth (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28, sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 2-4) |
| Alumina + Carbon | ~1800–>2000 | Carbothermal reduction and vapor-phase mass transfer; Al2O3 reacts with C-bearing surroundings, producing gaseous Al, Al2O, CO and condensed carbide; with excess carbon, liquid formation can occur through Al2O3–Al4C3-related eutectics | Al4C3, Al(g), Al2O(g), CO(g); Al2O3–Al4C3 eutectic liquids near 2220–2273 K (~1947–2000°C) | Al2O3 is not inert to carbon/graphite in this range; it can be chemically consumed and may form liquid phases near ~1950°C, compromising crucible integrity and contaminating the charge (baud2003hightemperaturesintering pages 1-2, inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 26-30) |
| Zirconia + Carbon | ~1200–1800+ | Carbothermal reduction of zirconia by carbon; idealized stoichiometry 3C + ZrO2 = ZrC + 2CO; ZrC appears by ~1200°C and reduction is largely complete by ~1400–1500°C, with lower oxygen retained only after hotter treatment | ZrC, CO; intermediate zirconium oxycarbide/oxygen-containing ZrC at lower T | ZrO2 is consumed by carbon rather than remaining a passive ceramic barrier; graphite contact will progressively convert/stain/consume zirconia and generate CO, so ZrO2 is a poor long-duration choice against carbon at these temperatures (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 2-3, sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 10-10, sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 3-5) |
| Tantalum + Boron Nitride | ~1700–2500 | Direct high-T interface compatibility is limited; Ta can react with BN at interfaces by taking up B and N from BN, with likely interfacial boride/nitride formation under sufficiently reducing/high-T conditions | Likely TaB2 and TaN/Ta–B–N interfacial products | Treat Ta–BN contact as metastable rather than inert in the upper part of this temperature range; BN can be useful as a separator, but direct long-duration Ta/BN contact should be minimized where contamination or interfacial embrittlement matters (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 5-7, sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 1-2) |
| Tantalum + MgO | ~1700–2500 | Oxygen abstraction/reduction tendency driven by Ta’s strong oxygen affinity; interfacial degradation is expected thermodynamically when Ta contacts oxide ceramics at very high T and low oxygen potential | Ta oxides/suboxides or dissolved O in Ta; locally reduced MgO-derived interface | MgO is not reliably inert against Ta in strongly reducing, high-T furnaces; Ta can getter oxygen from MgO, degrading the interface and altering local oxygen activity around the charge (glebovsky2015physicalandtechnological pages 10-13, inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 1-9) |
| Tantalum + Oxygen | ~600–2000+ (most relevant above ~1200) | Strong oxygen gettering by dissolution and oxide formation; in vacuum/high T, Ta reacts with oxygen to form volatile oxides and dissolved O, with time-dependent sublimation behavior unlike W/Mo | TaO, TaO2, other volatile Ta oxides; dissolved O in Ta | Ta strongly lowers oxygen potential in enclosed hot zones, which can protect oxygen-sensitive charges but also destabilize nearby oxides and alter chemistry; at higher T it can suffer mass loss through volatile oxide formation (glebovsky2015physicalandtechnological pages 10-13, inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 35-38, inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 30-35) |
| Ta vapor transport → deposition on ceramic specimens | ~1700–2500 (especially in low-pO2/high-vacuum hot zones) | Transport occurs via volatile Ta oxide species formed at hot Ta surfaces, followed by condensation/deposition on cooler nearby ceramic parts/specimens | Deposited Ta-bearing films or particulates derived from volatile TaO/TaO2 transport | Even without direct contact, Ta hardware can contaminate nearby ceramics/specimens by vapor transport; shielding, temperature management, and minimizing oxidizing impurities are important when purity is critical (inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 35-38, inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 30-35) |


*Table: This table summarizes the main high-temperature reactions among tantalum, carbon, BN, MgO, alumina, zirconia, and oxygen that matter for crucibles and susceptors. It is useful for quickly identifying which material pairings are chemically risky in the 1700–2500°C regime.*

## 2. Carburization of Tantalum: TaC and Ta₂C Formation

When tantalum is exposed to carbon or graphite at temperatures in the 1700–2500 °C range, reactive diffusion leads to the sequential formation of Ta₂C and TaC phases (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28). This process is so rapid at these temperatures that practical crystal growth systems deliberately pre-carbonize tantalum crucibles before use: the resulting TaC–Ta₂C ceramic coating is thermally and chemically stable, capable of enduring over 3000 hours of cumulative service in graphite-heated furnaces at 1800–2000 °C (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28). In AlN sublimation growth, for example, bulk crystal growth is performed at 1800–1900 °C in TaC crucibles under nitrogen atmosphere, and the protective TaC layer is converted into TaCN during the growth process (sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 2-4). The pre-carbonization coating also prevents the formation of low-melting-temperature eutectics between bare tantalum and silicon or aluminum species (Ta–Si, Ta–Al), which would otherwise be highly detrimental (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28, sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 5-7). However, even with TaC-coated crucibles in a graphite heater environment, carbon diffusion into the growing crystal remains a persistent source of contamination, with EPMA measurements showing carbon concentrations of several atomic percent in crystals grown in such setups (sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 5-7).

## 3. Alumina–Carbon Reactions and Eutectics Near 1800 °C

Alumina is not inert in contact with carbon or carbon-bearing atmospheres at temperatures above approximately 1800 °C. Thermodynamic analysis of the SiC–Al₂O₃ system by Baud et al. shows that the principal high-temperature vaporization reaction is 2 SiC(s) + Al₂O₃(s) + Al₂O(g) → 2 SiO(g) + 2 CO(g) + 4 Al(g), and that the vaporization is congruent between 1200 and 2170 K but becomes non-congruent above 2170 K when liquid silicon forms (baud2003hightemperaturesintering pages 1-2, baud2003hightemperaturesintering pages 5-7). In the presence of excess carbon, the alumina–aluminum carbide (Al₂O₃–Al₄C₃) system exhibits eutectic liquid formation between 2220 and 2273 K (~1947–2000 °C), and a ternary Al₂O₃–Al₄C₃–SiC liquid phase is also possible (baud2003hightemperaturesintering pages 1-2). These reactions mean that alumina crucibles or insulation in contact with graphite susceptors or carbon-containing atmospheres may suffer progressive degradation, weight loss via volatile Al₂O(g) and CO(g) transport, and even liquid formation at temperatures approaching 2000 °C. Vapor transport of Al₂O(g) and Al(g) can also lead to contamination of nearby specimens or growing crystals (baud2003hightemperaturesintering pages 2-3).

## 4. Carbothermal Reduction and Consumption of Zirconia by Carbon

Zirconia is consumed by carbon through the well-characterized carbothermal reduction reaction: 3C(s) + ZrO₂(s) = ZrC(s) + 2CO(g) (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 2-3). Using solution-derived precursors that achieve nanometer-level mixing, Sacks et al. demonstrated that ZrC formation becomes evident at temperatures as low as 1200 °C and the reaction is substantially complete by 1400–1500 °C (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 10-10, sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 1-2). The process proceeds through an intermediate zirconium oxycarbide phase, ZrO_yC_(1+y−x), with the generalized reaction ZrO_yC_(1+y−x)(s) + xC(s) = ZrC(s) + yCO(g) (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 5-7). Oxygen content in the ZrC product decreases progressively with temperature; at 1800 °C, nearly stoichiometric ZrC with only ~0.1 wt% oxygen is obtained (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 3-5). The crystallite growth follows a "contracting volume" model where the ZrC shell grows inward from the surface of ZrO₂ particles (sacks2004carbothermalreductionsynthesis pages 5-7). These findings demonstrate that zirconia crucibles or insulation in direct contact with graphite or carbon-rich environments at temperatures above ~1200 °C will be progressively consumed, making ZrO₂ a poor choice for long-duration containment against carbon at the temperatures of interest.

## 5. Tantalum–Boron Nitride Interface Degradation

Boron nitride is commonly employed in high-temperature furnace assemblies as a separator, insulator, or structural element alongside tantalum crucibles. While BN possesses excellent thermal shock resistance and chemical inertness in many environments, direct prolonged contact between Ta and BN at temperatures above ~1700 °C can lead to interfacial reaction. In AlN crystal growth systems, the combination of TaC crucibles with graphite and nitrogen environments has been extensively studied, and the general principle that refractory metals react with BN to form borides and/or nitrides at extreme temperatures is well established (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 5-7, sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 2-4). For practical crystal growth, tungsten crucibles are avoided with SiC seeds because Si in SiC reacts with W to form low-temperature tungsten silicide eutectics; instead, TaC crucibles are preferred (sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 5-7). The Ta–BN interface should be treated as metastable at temperatures above 1700 °C, and direct long-duration contact should be minimized where contamination or interfacial embrittlement is a concern.

## 6. Tantalum–MgO Interface Degradation

The strong oxygen affinity of tantalum, with a binding energy of Q_O = 166–179 kcal/g-atom (glebovsky2015physicalandtechnological pages 10-13), means that tantalum in contact with oxide ceramics such as MgO can abstract oxygen from the ceramic at high temperatures. This thermodynamic driving force for reduction of MgO at the Ta–MgO interface is expected to lead to progressive degradation, particularly under reducing conditions or in vacuum at temperatures above 1700 °C. The Inouye review of refractory metal–gas interactions confirms that tantalum alloys containing reactive alloying elements (Ti, Zr, Hf) show enhanced oxygen uptake compared to unalloyed metals (inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 26-30), and the same oxygen gettering tendency would apply at metal–oxide interfaces. While MgO has one of the highest melting points among oxide ceramics (~2852 °C), its stability against reduction by tantalum at the interface limits its reliability as a crucible material in direct contact with tantalum hardware.

## 7. Tantalum Vapor Transport and Deposition on Ceramic Specimens

At temperatures from approximately 1200 °C upward in vacuum environments, tantalum reacts with residual oxygen to form volatile oxide species, principally TaO(g) and TaO₂(g) (inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 30-35). Unlike tungsten and molybdenum, which show constant sublimation rates at given temperature and pressure, the sublimation rate of tantalum varies markedly with time due to the competition between oxygen dissolution into the metal bulk and volatile oxide formation at the surface (inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 35-38). As oxygen progressively saturates the near-surface region, the volatile oxide generation rate increases until reaching a plateau. These volatile tantalum oxide species can be transported through the gas phase and deposited on cooler surfaces, contaminating nearby ceramic specimens or growing crystals. The pressures of volatile tantalum oxides as a function of temperature have been characterized at oxygen pressures of ~1.7 × 10⁻⁷ torr, with the generation rates passing through characteristic maxima that are temperature-dependent (inouye1968interactionsofrefractory pages 30-35).

## 8. Oxygen Gettering by Tantalum

Tantalum is one of the strongest oxygen getters among the refractory metals. In the solid state, tantalum desorbs oxygen primarily as monoxide (TaO) and dioxide (TaO₂) species, with an evaporation ratio of 28–42, indicating that oxygen can be removed by high-temperature vacuum annealing (glebovsky2015physicalandtechnological pages 10-13). Above the melting point of tantalum, the evaporation ratio increases dramatically to 2000–3000, reflecting intensive oxygen removal from the molten state (glebovsky2015physicalandtechnological pages 10-13). This oxygen gettering capability has dual practical implications: on one hand, tantalum components in a furnace can serve as sacrificial getters that lower the oxygen partial pressure and protect oxygen-sensitive materials; on the other hand, oxygen abstracted from nearby oxide ceramics (MgO, Al₂O₃, ZrO₂) can destabilize those ceramics and alter the local chemical environment. For AlN crystal growth, the presence of oxygen is particularly detrimental due to the formation of oxynitrides and stacking faults that decrease thermal conductivity and introduce sub-band-gap optical absorption (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28). Hence, tantalum's gettering effect must be carefully managed in systems where both tantalum components and oxide ceramics are present.

## 9. Practical Implications and Material Selection

The two-stage crucible technology developed for AlN sublimation growth illustrates how these compatibility constraints are managed in practice: initial seeding and growth on SiC substrates is performed at 1800–1900 °C in pre-carbonized TaC crucibles within graphite RF-heated furnaces, while subsequent bulk crystal growth at 2050–2250 °C uses tungsten crucibles in tungsten resistively heated furnaces to eliminate carbon contamination (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28, avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 28-35). The pre-carbonized TaC–Ta₂C coating on tantalum crucibles endures cumulative service exceeding 3000 hours, preventing the formation of detrimental Ta–Si and Ta–Al eutectics (avdeev2012developmentof2" pages 25-28). Carbon contamination from the graphite heater environment remains a persistent issue, with Si and C impurities reaching several atomic percent in AlN crystals grown in graphite-equipped systems (sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 5-7, sumathi2021commonissuesin pages 9-11).

|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Tantalum + Graphite/Carbon | ~1700–2500 | Reactive diffusion/carburization of Ta in C-rich environments; pre-carbonization intentionally forms protective carbide layers on Ta crucibles, typically TaC/Ta2C, and suppresses direct Ta–Si and Ta–Al eutectic attack | TaC, Ta2C, sometimes TaCN during nitride growth service | Bare Ta is not compatible with graphite at these temperatures for long exposure; carburized/TaC-coated Ta is much more stable and is therefore used as crucible or liner material in high-T nitride crystal growth (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000002) |
| Alumina + Carbon | ~1800–>2000 | Carbothermal reduction and vapor-phase mass transfer; Al2O3 reacts with C-bearing surroundings, producing gaseous Al, Al2O, CO and condensed carbide; with excess carbon, liquid formation can occur through Al2O3–Al4C3-related eutectics | Al4C3, Al(g), Al2O(g), CO(g); Al2O3–Al4C3 eutectic liquids near 2220–2273 K (~1947–2000°C) | Al2O3 is not inert to carbon/graphite in this range; it can be chemically consumed and may form liquid phases near ~1950°C, compromising crucible integrity and contaminating the charge (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027) |
| Zirconia + Carbon | ~1200–1800+ | Carbothermal reduction of zirconia by carbon; idealized stoichiometry 3C + ZrO2 = ZrC + 2CO; ZrC appears by ~1200°C and reduction is largely complete by ~1400–1500°C, with lower oxygen retained only after hotter treatment | ZrC, CO; intermediate zirconium oxycarbide/oxygen-containing ZrC at lower T | ZrO2 is consumed by carbon rather than remaining a passive ceramic barrier; graphite contact will progressively convert/stain/consume zirconia and generate CO, so ZrO2 is a poor long-duration choice against carbon at these temperatures (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040) |
| Tantalum + Boron Nitride | ~1700–2500 | Direct high-T interface compatibility is limited; Ta can react with BN at interfaces by taking up B and N from BN, with likely interfacial boride/nitride formation under sufficiently reducing/high-T conditions | Likely TaB2 and TaN/Ta–B–N interfacial products | Treat Ta–BN contact as metastable rather than inert in the upper part of this temperature range; BN can be useful as a separator, but direct long-duration Ta/BN contact should be minimized where contamination or interfacial embrittlement matters (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000003) |
| Tantalum + MgO | ~1700–2500 | Oxygen abstraction/reduction tendency driven by Ta’s strong oxygen affinity; interfacial degradation is expected thermodynamically when Ta contacts oxide ceramics at very high T and low oxygen potential | Ta oxides/suboxides or dissolved O in Ta; locally reduced MgO-derived interface | MgO is not reliably inert against Ta in strongly reducing, high-T furnaces; Ta can getter oxygen from MgO, degrading the interface and altering local oxygen activity around the charge (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000001) |
| Tantalum + Oxygen | ~600–2000+ (most relevant above ~1200) | Strong oxygen gettering by dissolution and oxide formation; in vacuum/high T, Ta reacts with oxygen to form volatile oxides and dissolved O, with time-dependent sublimation behavior unlike W/Mo | TaO, TaO2, other volatile Ta oxides; dissolved O in Ta | Ta strongly lowers oxygen potential in enclosed hot zones, which can protect oxygen-sensitive charges but also destabilize nearby oxides and alter chemistry; at higher T it can suffer mass loss through volatile oxide formation (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) |
| Ta vapor transport → deposition on ceramic specimens | ~1700–2500 (especially in low-pO2/high-vacuum hot zones) | Transport occurs via volatile Ta oxide species formed at hot Ta surfaces, followed by condensation/deposition on cooler nearby ceramic parts/specimens | Deposited Ta-bearing films or particulates derived from volatile TaO/TaO2 transport | Even without direct contact, Ta hardware can contaminate nearby ceramics/specimens by vapor transport; shielding, temperature management, and minimizing oxidizing impurities are important when purity is critical (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) |

info.query: Review high-temperature (1700-2500 C) chemical compatibility among refractory materials used as crucibles and susceptors: tantalum, graphite/carbon, boron nitride, magnesia (MgO), alumina, and zirconia. Include carburization of tantalum (TaC formation), alumina-carbon reactions and eutectics near 1800 C, carbothermal reduction/consumption of zirconia by carbon, Ta-BN and Ta-MgO interface degradation, interdiffusion and vapor transport (Ta deposition on ceramic specimens), and oxygen gettering by tantalum. Cite high-quality sources with bibtex.
